## Why This Matters

Every algorithm so far -- regression, logistic regression, trees, neural networks -- needed an
answer key: a labeled `y` to learn from. But most data in the world arrives **unlabeled**.
Customers with no segment, photos with no caption, sensor logs with no fault tag. **Unsupervised
learning** asks the question that does not need a teacher: *given only `X`, what structure is
already in the data?*

The first and most common answer is **clustering** -- put similar things together -- and the
whole game turns on one word: **similar**. K-Means gives the simplest possible meaning to it
("close to the same center") and rides that single idea to a fast, scalable algorithm that
powers customer segmentation, image compression, and anomaly detection. We build it, learn to
choose how many clusters to ask for, and then find exactly where its simplicity gives out.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Imagine dropping 1500 pins on a map and being told to mark four "neighborhoods," with no
addresses or names to go on. You would plant four flags, assign each pin to its nearest flag,
then move each flag to the middle of the pins that chose it -- and repeat until the flags settle.
That is K-Means exactly. "Similar" means "nearest flag"; a neighborhood is just whoever is
closest to the same center.
:::

## From Labels to Structure

Supervised learning fit a map from `X` to a known `y`. Unsupervised learning is handed only
`X` and must find structure on its own. **Clustering** is the canonical task: partition the
points into groups so that members of a group are more similar to each other than to members of
other groups. There is no single right answer and no accuracy to report -- different notions of
"similar" yield different, equally valid clusterings.

Clustering shows up everywhere: **customer segmentation** (group buyers by behavior),
**anomaly detection** (a point far from every cluster is suspicious), **image compression**
(replace each pixel with its cluster's mean color), and **semi-supervised learning** (cluster,
then propagate a handful of labels within each group). All of them rest on the same primitive:
a way to measure similarity.

## Similarity Is Distance

For K-Means, "similar" means one specific thing: **small Euclidean distance**. The distance
between points $x$ and $x'$ in feature space is

$$
d(x, x') = \lVert x - x' \rVert = \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_j (x_j - x'_j)^2},
$$

and a point belongs to whichever **centroid** -- cluster center -- it is closest to. In the lab,
`transform` reports each point's distance to every centroid, and we turn distance into an
**affinity** with $1/(1+d)$: 1 when you sit on the centroid, fading to 0 as you move away.

This is a choice, not a law. Other algorithms use other notions of similarity -- connected
density (DBSCAN) or a linkage rule between whole clusters (hierarchical) -- and they find
different kinds of groups. That is L24. K-Means' commitment to "distance to a center" is both
its speed and its blind spot.

## K-Means: The Lloyd Iteration

Given a chosen number of clusters `k`, K-Means runs a beautifully simple loop:

1. **Initialize** `k` centroids (k-means++ picks spread-out starting points -- see below).
2. **Assign** each point to its nearest centroid (the Euclidean similarity rule).
3. **Update** each centroid to the **mean** of the points now assigned to it.
4. Repeat steps 2-3 until the assignments stop changing.

That is it -- alternate "assign to nearest" and "recenter on the mean." This is **Lloyd's
algorithm**, and it is guaranteed to **converge**: each step can only lower the **inertia** (the
within-cluster sum of squared distances), and inertia cannot go below zero, so the loop must
settle.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  I["Initialize k centroids<br/>(k-means++)"] --> A["Assign each point to<br/>its nearest centroid"]
  A --> U["Update each centroid to the<br/>mean of its assigned points"]
  U --> Q{"Did any<br/>assignment change?"}
  Q -- "yes" --> A
  Q -- "no" --> D["Converged:<br/>final clusters + centroids"]
```

$$
\text{inertia} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \; \sum_{x \in C_i} \lVert x - c_i \rVert^2
\qquad (C_i = \text{cluster } i,\; c_i = \text{its centroid})
$$

**Convergence is not optimality.** Lloyd settles to a *local* minimum that depends on where the
centroids started. A bad initialization can leave two centroids splitting one true blob while
another blob goes unclaimed. Two standard guards: **k-means++** initialization (picks starting
centroids far apart -- scikit-learn's default) and **`n_init`** (run the whole thing several
times from different starts and keep the lowest-inertia result, also the default).

## How Many Clusters?

K-Means cannot tell you `k`; you must supply it. The tempting idea -- pick the `k` with the
smallest inertia -- **fails**, because inertia *only ever decreases* as `k` grows (more centroids
always sit closer to the points; at `k = n` it reaches zero). Two honest tools instead:

- **The elbow method.** Plot inertia against `k` and look for the bend where the steep drop
  flattens out. In the lab, inertia plunges from 14371 to 1352 by `k=4`, then crawls -- the
  elbow sits at **k=4**, the true number of blobs. The elbow is read by eye, so it is a guide,
  not a verdict.
- **The silhouette score.** For each point, compare its mean distance to its own cluster ($a$)
  against its mean distance to the nearest *other* cluster ($b$); the point's silhouette
  coefficient is $(b - a)/\max(a, b)$, between $-1$ and $+1$. The **silhouette score** is the
  average over all points, and the best `k` is the one that **maximizes** it. In the lab it
  peaks cleanly at **k=4 (0.627)** -- a quantitative answer where the elbow only suggested one.

$$
s(x) = \frac{b - a}{\max(a, b)} \qquad
\begin{cases} \;\to +1 & \text{deep inside its cluster} \\ \;\to 0 & \text{on a boundary} \\ \;\to -1 & \text{likely mis-assigned} \end{cases}
$$

The silhouette is more expensive (it weighs every point against every cluster) but, unlike
inertia, it does not simply reward more clusters -- so it can actually choose.

## When K-Means Breaks

K-Means' single tool -- distance to a center -- carries a hidden assumption: clusters are
**round, similar-size, similar-density blobs**. When that holds, it is fast and excellent (in the
lab it matches the true grouping at ARI 0.962). When it does not, it fails, and the failures are
predictable:

- **Unscaled features.** Distance is dominated by whatever feature has the largest numeric range.
  If one feature runs 0-1000 and another 0-1, K-Means effectively ignores the small one. In the
  lab, the same data clusters at ARI 0.334 raw versus **1.0 after `StandardScaler`** -- always
  scale first (the standardization of L08/L10).
- **Non-spherical shapes.** Two interleaved crescents have a clear structure, but K-Means can
  only carve space with straight boundaries around centers, so it slices each crescent in half.
  In the lab it collapses from ARI 0.962 on blobs to **0.239 on two moons**.
- **Varying sizes or densities.** A tight dense cluster next to a large sparse one confuses the
  "nearest center" rule, which has no concept of density.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  S{"What do the clusters<br/>look like?"}
  S -- "round, similar-size blobs;<br/>you can guess k" --> K["K-Means<br/>(fast, scalable; scale first)"]
  S -- "arbitrary shapes, or k unknown,<br/>or you need outliers flagged" --> O["Density / hierarchical<br/>clustering -> L24"]
```

That last failure -- the crescents -- is the cliffhanger into **L24**, where DBSCAN clusters by
connected density and hierarchical clustering merges by linkage, both wrapping the shapes K-Means
cuts in two.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Reading meaning into cluster numbers.** The labels `0,1,2,3` are arbitrary tags; cluster `0`
  in one run may be cluster `2` in the next. Compare clusterings by their grouping, not their
  integers.
- **Picking `k` by minimizing inertia.** Inertia always falls with more clusters -- it bottoms out
  at `k = n`. Use the elbow or the silhouette instead.
- **Forgetting to scale.** K-Means is a distance algorithm; an unscaled large-range feature
  hijacks every assignment. Standardize first.
- **Trusting one random start.** A single initialization can land in a bad local optimum; rely on
  k-means++ and `n_init` (both on by default in scikit-learn).
- **Forcing K-Means on the wrong shape.** If the groups are elongated, nested, or wildly
  different in density, no amount of tuning fixes the round-blob assumption -- change the
  algorithm.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why inertia can only fall (Optional)" collapse="true"}

Each Lloyd step lowers inertia for two reasons. The **assignment** step moves every point to its
nearest centroid, which can only shrink (or hold) that point's squared distance. The **update**
step sets each centroid to the mean of its cluster, and the mean is exactly the point that
minimizes the sum of squared distances to a set of points. So both steps are downhill on the
same objective, inertia is bounded below by 0, and the iteration converges -- to a *local*
minimum, which is why initialization (k-means++, `n_init`) matters. Adding a cluster gives the
optimizer strictly more freedom, so the best achievable inertia can only drop as `k` rises --
exactly why you cannot select `k` by minimizing it.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"How do I choose `k` in practice?"** -- Combine signals: run the silhouette score across a
range of `k`, sanity-check with the elbow, and weigh domain knowledge (you often *know* you want
"3 customer tiers"). The silhouette is the most reliable single number, but clustering is
exploratory -- there is rarely one correct `k`.

**"K-Means or something fancier?"** -- K-Means first: it is fast, scalable, and excellent when
clusters are roughly round and you can guess `k`. Reach for DBSCAN (L24) when shapes are
arbitrary or you need outliers flagged, hierarchical clustering when you want a full merge tree,
and Gaussian mixtures (L25) when you want soft, probabilistic memberships.

**"Is clustering the same as classification?"** -- No. Classification learns a labeled `y` and
predicts it; clustering invents groups from `X` alone with no ground truth. You can *use* clusters
as features or pseudo-labels afterward, but the clustering step itself is unsupervised.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Unsupervised learning | find structure in `X` with no labels `y` |
| Clustering | partition points into similar groups; labels are arbitrary integers |
| Similarity (K-Means) | Euclidean **distance to a centroid**; affinity = 1/(1+d) |
| Lloyd iteration | assign to nearest centroid, recenter on the mean, repeat to convergence |
| Inertia | within-cluster sum of squared distances; K-Means minimizes it; always falls with `k` |
| Choosing `k` | the **elbow** (bend in inertia) and the **silhouette score** (maximize it) |
| k-means++ / `n_init` | spread-out init + multiple restarts to dodge bad local optima |
| Scaling | mandatory -- the largest-range feature hijacks distance otherwise |
| Failure mode | round-blob assumption: breaks on crescents/elongated/varying-density (-> L24) |
